entry.summary:

Source: @hesmashena

I suspect it is precisely at this point that the headline can outrun the text. The core message is not necessarily that Iran is more powerful than America, China, or any other power. The core message is that Iran today, in the narrative being presented, is not an Iran that can be dragged back to its former position of dependency. This is no small distinction. In the text, three temporal planes are woven together: a past that must not return, a present that must be defended, and a future that must be more powerful than the present. That is why the message does not conclude in the past either; it moves toward the future. But it is precisely here that the most difficult question begins. "We will not go back" is not merely a statement about a foreign enemy. Not going back cannot be measured solely by missile range, the distance of enemy warships, or military operational capacity. If we take the concept of power seriously, then the economy, knowledge, technology, the quality of governance, public trust, human capital, social cohesion, and the ability to solve problems are all part of that same arena. A country that does not want to go back must be able to simultaneously withstand external threats and, on the domestic front, create the capacity for a better life, greater hope, and the possibility of broader progress. This is where the narrative of power meets people's everyday experience. The narrower the gap between the two, the more the phrase "we will not go back" transforms from a political slogan into a collective experience. The wider this gap grows, the less the foreign enemy even needs to challenge the narrative; people's daily lives will do it for them. The recent message can be read from various angles. One can debate its claim to power, the Strait of Hormuz, regional resistance, or its religious symbolism. But the thread binding all these elements together is, to my mind, too clear to be lost in noisy headlines: "The enemy wants Iran to return to the past; the text says that past is over." The question of Iran's future lies in exactly the same place: let us not go back — not only in independence and security, but in every component that truly makes a nation powerful.
